title: CASE Expressions
summary: Choose a value row by row with CASE, SQL's if, else, and switch.
intro: Sometimes a column needs a different value depending on the row: a letter for a score, a plan for a priority. `CASE` is SQL's if and else, and it works anywhere a value does, even in `ORDER BY`.
setup:
CREATE TABLE students (id integer, name text, score integer);
INSERT INTO students (id, name, score) VALUES
    (1, 'Ana', 92),
    (2, 'Ben', 85),
    (3, 'Cara', 78),
    (4, 'Dev', 64),
    (5, 'Eli', 95),
    (6, 'Fay', 70),
    (7, 'Gus', 59);

CREATE TABLE tickets (id integer, title text, priority text, status text);
INSERT INTO tickets (id, title, priority, status) VALUES
    (1, 'Login page crashes', 'high', 'open'),
    (2, 'Typo in footer', 'low', 'done'),
    (3, 'Slow search', 'medium', 'in progress'),
    (4, 'Export to CSV', 'medium', 'open'),
    (5, 'Password reset email', 'high', 'in progress'),
    (6, 'Dark mode colors', 'low', 'open');

steps.title: If and else with CASE WHEN
steps.body:
This lesson uses two small tables: students with a test score, and support tickets.

```sql
CREATE TABLE students (id integer, name text, score integer);
CREATE TABLE tickets (id integer, title text, priority text, status text);
```

A `CASE` expression picks a value for each row, like if, else if, and else. PostgreSQL checks the `WHEN` conditions from top to bottom and returns the `THEN` value of the **first** true one. The rest are skipped, so put the strictest test first: if `score >= 80` came before `score >= 90`, a 95 would get a B.

```sql
CASE
    WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A'
    WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'B'
    ELSE 'F'
END AS grade
```

`ELSE` catches every row no branch matched, including a `NULL` score, since a comparison with `NULL` is never true. Leave `ELSE` out and those rows get `NULL`, which prints as nothing. Name the column with `AS`, or psql heads it `case`. All branches must give one type. Mixing a number and text fails, because PostgreSQL tries to read the text as a number:

```sql
CASE WHEN score >= 60 THEN score ELSE 'none' END
```

```text
ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "none"
```

example.title: Grade letters
example.prompt: Turn each student's score into a letter grade.
example.code:
SELECT name, score,
    CASE
        WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A'
        WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'B'
        WHEN score >= 70 THEN 'C'
        ELSE 'F'
    END AS grade
FROM students
ORDER BY id;
example.output:
name | score | grade
------+-------+-------
 Ana  |    92 | A
 Ben  |    85 | B
 Cara |    78 | C
 Dev  |    64 | F
 Eli  |    95 | A
 Fay  |    70 | C
 Gus  |    59 | F
(7 rows)
example.explanation: For each row, PostgreSQL tries the `WHEN` conditions from the top. Ana's 92 passes `score >= 90`, so she gets `A` and the rest are skipped. Cara's 78 fails the first two and passes `score >= 70`. Fay's 70 sits exactly on the boundary and `>=` includes it, so she gets `C`. Dev and Gus match nothing, so `ELSE` gives them `F`.

practice.title: Pass, fail, or distinction
practice.prompt:
Label each student's result as distinction, pass, or fail.

1. Select `name` and `score` from `students`.
2. Add a column named `result`: `distinction` for a score of 95 or more, `pass` for 60 or more, and `fail` for anything else, including a missing score.
3. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
 name | score |   result
------+-------+-------------
 Ana  |    92 | pass
 Ben  |    85 | pass
 Cara |    78 | pass
 Dev  |    64 | pass
 Eli  |    95 | distinction
 Fay  |    70 | pass
 Gus  |    59 | fail
(7 rows)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT name, score
    -- TODO: add a CASE column named result
FROM students
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT name, score,
    CASE
        WHEN score >= 95 THEN 'distinction'
        WHEN score >= 60 THEN 'pass'
        ELSE 'fail'
    END AS result
FROM students
ORDER BY id;

tests.output:
name | score |   result
------+-------+-------------
 Ana  |    92 | pass
 Ben  |    85 | pass
 Cara |    78 | pass
 Dev  |    64 | pass
 Eli  |    95 | distinction
 Fay  |    70 | pass
 Gus  |    59 | fail
(7 rows)

tests.stdin: INSERT INTO students (id, name, score) VALUES (8, 'Hana', 60), (9, 'Ivo', 94), (10, 'Jun', 100);
tests.output:
name | score |   result
------+-------+-------------
 Ana  |    92 | pass
 Ben  |    85 | pass
 Cara |    78 | pass
 Dev  |    64 | pass
 Eli  |    95 | distinction
 Fay  |    70 | pass
 Gus  |    59 | fail
 Hana |    60 | pass
 Ivo  |    94 | pass
 Jun  |   100 | distinction
(10 rows)

tests.stdin:
DELETE FROM students WHERE id > 2;
INSERT INTO students (id, name, score) VALUES (3, 'Kai', 59), (4, 'Lea', 96), (5, 'Max', 61), (6, 'Nia', NULL);
tests.output:
name | score |   result
------+-------+-------------
 Ana  |    92 | pass
 Ben  |    85 | pass
 Kai  |    59 | fail
 Lea  |    96 | distinction
 Max  |    61 | pass
 Nia  |       | fail
(6 rows)

hints: Put the strictest condition first. If `score >= 60` came first, a 95 would stop there and get `pass`.
A missing score fails every comparison, so `ELSE` already gives it `fail`.
The shape is `CASE WHEN ... THEN 'distinction' WHEN ... THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END AS result`.

steps.title: Matching values like a switch
steps.body:
The `tickets` table holds six support tickets. Each has a `priority` (`high`, `medium`, or `low`) and a `status` (`open`, `in progress`, or `done`):

```text
 id |       title        | priority |   status
----+--------------------+----------+-------------
  1 | Login page crashes | high     | open
  2 | Typo in footer     | low      | done
  3 | Slow search        | medium   | in progress
```

When every branch compares one column with a fixed value, use the **simple** form, like a switch statement. Name the value right after `CASE`, then list the matches:

```sql
CASE priority
    WHEN 'high' THEN 'fix today'
    WHEN 'medium' THEN 'this week'
    ELSE 'someday'
END AS plan
```

It means the same as `CASE WHEN priority = 'high' THEN ...`, with less typing. The simple form only tests equality, so ranges like `score >= 90` still need `CASE WHEN`. One gotcha: `WHEN NULL` never matches, because `NULL = NULL` is not true. Let `ELSE` catch missing values, or use `CASE WHEN status IS NULL THEN ...`.

example.title: Plans by priority
example.prompt: Turn each ticket's priority into a plan for when to fix it.
example.code:
SELECT title, priority,
    CASE priority
        WHEN 'high' THEN 'fix today'
        WHEN 'medium' THEN 'this week'
        ELSE 'someday'
    END AS plan
FROM tickets
ORDER BY id;
example.output:
title         | priority |   plan
----------------------+----------+-----------
 Login page crashes   | high     | fix today
 Typo in footer       | low      | someday
 Slow search          | medium   | this week
 Export to CSV        | medium   | this week
 Password reset email | high     | fix today
 Dark mode colors     | low      | someday
(6 rows)
example.explanation: `CASE priority` names the value once, and each `WHEN` lists a value to compare it with using `=`. The two `high` tickets match the first branch and the two `medium` ones the second. Nothing matches `low`, so those rows fall to `ELSE` and get `someday`.

practice.title: Status labels
practice.prompt:
Give each ticket a friendly label for its status.

1. Select `title` and `status` from `tickets`.
2. Add a column named `label` using a simple `CASE` on `status`: `open` becomes `to do`, `in progress` becomes `doing`, `done` becomes `finished`, and anything else, including a missing status, becomes `unknown`.
3. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
        title         |   status    |  label
----------------------+-------------+----------
 Login page crashes   | open        | to do
 Typo in footer       | done        | finished
 Slow search          | in progress | doing
 Export to CSV        | open        | to do
 Password reset email | in progress | doing
 Dark mode colors     | open        | to do
(6 rows)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT title, status
    -- TODO: add a simple CASE column named label
FROM tickets
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT title, status,
    CASE status
        WHEN 'open' THEN 'to do'
        WHEN 'in progress' THEN 'doing'
        WHEN 'done' THEN 'finished'
        ELSE 'unknown'
    END AS label
FROM tickets
ORDER BY id;

tests.output:
title         |   status    |  label
----------------------+-------------+----------
 Login page crashes   | open        | to do
 Typo in footer       | done        | finished
 Slow search          | in progress | doing
 Export to CSV        | open        | to do
 Password reset email | in progress | doing
 Dark mode colors     | open        | to do
(6 rows)

tests.stdin: INSERT INTO tickets (id, title, priority, status) VALUES (7, 'Broken link', 'low', 'done'), (8, 'Add search filters', 'medium', 'blocked'), (9, 'Crash on upload', 'high', NULL);
tests.output:
title         |   status    |  label
----------------------+-------------+----------
 Login page crashes   | open        | to do
 Typo in footer       | done        | finished
 Slow search          | in progress | doing
 Export to CSV        | open        | to do
 Password reset email | in progress | doing
 Dark mode colors     | open        | to do
 Broken link          | done        | finished
 Add search filters   | blocked     | unknown
 Crash on upload      |             | unknown
(9 rows)

tests.stdin:
DELETE FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open';
INSERT INTO tickets (id, title, priority, status) VALUES (10, 'Update logo', 'low', 'open');
tests.output:
title         |   status    |  label
----------------------+-------------+----------
 Typo in footer       | done        | finished
 Slow search          | in progress | doing
 Password reset email | in progress | doing
 Update logo          | open        | to do
(4 rows)

hints: Write `CASE status` once, then one `WHEN 'value' THEN 'label'` line per status.
A missing status never matches a `WHEN`, so `ELSE 'unknown'` covers it too.

steps.title: Custom sort orders
steps.body:
`ORDER BY priority` sorts text alphabetically, so you get `high`, `low`, `medium`. To sort in your own order, map each value to a number with `CASE` and sort by that number:

```sql
ORDER BY
    CASE priority
        WHEN 'high' THEN 1
        WHEN 'medium' THEN 2
        ELSE 3
    END,
    id
```

The `CASE` only decides the order, so it does not show up as a column. Values that get the same number tie, so add a unique column like `id` last. Put `DESC` after `END` to flip the order. You can also show the rank as a column, `... END AS rank`, and write `ORDER BY rank, id`. An alias works in `ORDER BY` only on its own, not inside a bigger expression.

example.title: Most urgent first
example.prompt: List the tickets with high priority first, then medium, then low.
example.code:
SELECT id, title, priority
FROM tickets
ORDER BY
    CASE priority
        WHEN 'high' THEN 1
        WHEN 'medium' THEN 2
        ELSE 3
    END,
    id;
example.output:
id |        title         | priority
----+----------------------+----------
  1 | Login page crashes   | high
  5 | Password reset email | high
  3 | Slow search          | medium
  4 | Export to CSV        | medium
  2 | Typo in footer       | low
  6 | Dark mode colors     | low
(6 rows)
example.explanation: The `CASE` turns each priority into a rank: 1, 2, or 3. Rows sort by that rank, so both `high` tickets come first. Tickets with the same rank tie, and `id` breaks the tie, which keeps 1 before 5 and 3 before 4.

practice.title: Open tickets first
practice.prompt:
List the tickets in the order a team would work through them by status.

1. Select `id`, `title`, and `status` from `tickets`.
2. Sort `open` tickets first, then `in progress`, then `done`, and any other status last.
3. Break ties by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
 id |        title         |   status
----+----------------------+-------------
  1 | Login page crashes   | open
  4 | Export to CSV        | open
  6 | Dark mode colors     | open
  3 | Slow search          | in progress
  5 | Password reset email | in progress
  2 | Typo in footer       | done
(6 rows)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT id, title, status
FROM tickets
ORDER BY id; -- TODO: sort by a CASE rank for status first, then id

FROM tickets
ORDER BY
    CASE status
        WHEN 'open' THEN 1
        WHEN 'in progress' THEN 2
        WHEN 'done' THEN 3
        ELSE 4
    END,
    id;

----+----------------------+-------------

  4 | Export to CSV        | open
  6 | Dark mode colors     | open
  3 | Slow search          | in progress

(6 rows)

Put the `CASE` right after `ORDER BY`, then a comma and `id` to break ties.

recap:
- `CASE WHEN condition THEN value ... ELSE value END` picks a value for each row.
- The first true `WHEN` wins, so put the strictest condition first.
- Without `ELSE`, a row that matches nothing gets `NULL`.
- `CASE column WHEN value THEN result ... END` is the simple form for matching exact values. It never matches `NULL`.
- `ORDER BY CASE ... END, id` sorts rows in any order you choose.
